- The statement of actuarial opinion must include six components: table of key indicators, identification section, scope section, reliance section, opinion section, and relevant comments section, each with prescribed wording that may be modified only with documented rationale.
- The opinion must cover all in-force business and address reserve adequacy under moderately adverse conditions, consistency with prior year methods, and compliance with state law.
- The supporting actuarial memorandum must document product descriptions, reserve methods, asset portfolios, assumptions (lapse, mortality, interest, expenses), analysis methodology, and material changes, and must be retained for at least seven years.
- A confidential Regulatory Asset Adequacy Issues Summary must be submitted annually to the domiciliary commissioner by April 1, detailing testing scenarios, assumption changes, and reinsurance treatment.

Conclusions and Implications: VM-30 standardizes the format, content, and professional responsibilities involved in certifying life insurance reserve adequacy, ensuring consistency across companies while preserving actuarial judgment. Compliance ensures regulatory transparency and confidentiality protections for sensitive analyses while enabling regulators to assess reserve sufficiency under adverse conditions.

202601 VM-31.pdf.summary:
Title: VM-31: PBR Actuarial Report Requirements for Business Subject to a Principle-Based Valuation

Publisher and Published Date: NAIC (National Association of Insurance Commissioners), Valuation Manual section (specific date not stated in excerpt)

Purpose and Scope: This section establishes minimum reporting requirements for life insurance policies and annuity contracts subject to principle-based valuation under VM-20, VM-21, and VM-22. It defines the structure, content, documentation, and filing requirements for the PBR Actuarial Report that companies must prepare annually.

Key Points:
- Applies to any company computing an exclusion test or minimum reserve under VM-20, VM-21, or VM-22, including those passing exclusion tests or using the VM-21 Alternative Methodology.
- The report must include an Executive Summary, Life Summary, Life Report, Annuity Summary, and Annuity Report, each prepared by qualified actuaries under VM-G governance provisions, with sufficient documentation for peer actuarial review.
- Executive Summary/Life Summary/Annuity Summary must be filed with the domiciliary commissioner by April 1 following the valuation year; full report submitted upon request within specified timeframes; records retained at least seven years.
- Detailed Life Report requirements cover assumptions/margins, mortality, policyholder behavior, expenses, assets, reinsurance, non-guaranteed elements, exclusion tests, sensitivity testing, and required certifications (investment officer, qualified actuary, senior management).
- Detailed Annuity Report requirements cover liabilities, cash-flow models, mortality/longevity, hedging and risk management (CDHS), scenario generation, reinsurance, Alternative Methodology, exclusion tests, and additional standard projection amount calculations.
- Reports must be submitted as searchable PDFs (10-point font minimum), with large data sets accompanied by spreadsheets considered part of the official report.

Conclusions and Implications: VM-31 ensures regulatory transparency and auditability of principle-based reserve calculations by mandating comprehensive, standardized documentation of assumptions, methods, models, and governance. Compliance enables regulators to evaluate reserve adequacy and consistency across companies, supporting oversight of complex stochastic and deterministic valuation approaches for life and annuity business.

202601 VM-50-51.pdf.summary:
Title: VM-50: Experience Reporting Requirements and VM-51: Experience Reporting Formats (NAIC Valuation Manual)

Publisher and Published Date: National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC); effective statistical plan data collection begins January 1, 2020

Purpose and Scope: These sections of the NAIC Valuation Manual establish requirements for collecting, validating, and using company experience data under Section 13 of Model #820 to support principle-based reserving (PBR). They define the roles of the Experience Reporting Agent, data quality and confidentiality standards (VM-50), and the specific statistical plan, data elements, and reporting formats for individual ordinary life mortality experience (VM-51).

Key Points:
- VM-50 establishes NAIC as the Experience Reporting Agent for the Statistical Plan for Mortality, responsible for collecting, validating, and aggregating company data into industry experience tables.
- Data quality controls include validity checks, reconciliation to statistical/financial data, reasonability checks, systematic error detection, and "critical indication" reporting requiring company response.
- Companies retain ownership of submitted data; confidentiality is governed by Model #820 Section 14A(5), restricting access to regulators, the submitting company, NAIC, auditors, and authorized contractors.
- VM-51 defines the mortality statistical plan scope (individual ordinary life, direct U.S. business), exemption thresholds ($50 million direct premium, with $10 million affiliate carve-out), and annual submission process via the RDC application.
- Reporting uses a calendar-year method with defined observation years, termination reporting rules, and deadlines (September 30 submission, February 28 corrections).
- Appendices provide standardized questionnaires (preferred class structure, mortality claims), additional plan code forms, and a detailed 47-item data element specification covering policy identifiers, demographics, underwriting, plan codes, face amounts, premiums, and secondary guarantee details for universal/variable life.

Conclusions and Implications: The framework ensures reliable, standardized, and confidential aggregation of company mortality experience to support development of industry mortality tables, PBR assumption-setting, and regulatory oversight. Companies subject to reporting must maintain data systems capable of producing detailed, reconciled experience records and promptly resolving identified data quality issues.

202601 VM-A.pdf.summary:
Title: VM-A: Appendix A - Requirements (Index of Referenced Requirements)

Publisher and Published Date: National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), Valuation Manual, date not specified in excerpt

Purpose and Scope: This document serves as an appendix within the Valuation Manual (VM-A) that indexes requirements incorporated by reference from Appendix A of the NAIC's Accounting Practices & Procedures (AP&P) Manual. It functions as a navigational and cross-reference tool identifying which specific model regulations and requirements apply to various insurance product types and actuarial valuation topics.

Key Points:
- The appendix lists 18 distinct requirements, each identified by a reference number (e.g., A-200, A-250, A-820) and corresponding title.
- Covered topics include separate accounts for guaranteed minimum benefits, interest-indexed annuities, variable annuities and life insurance, modified guaranteed annuities and life insurance, universal life insurance, and accelerated benefits.
- Mortality table standards are addressed through multiple references, including smoker/nonsmoker tables (A-812), 2001 CSO mortality table recognition (VM-A-814), preferred mortality tables (A-815), and annuity mortality tables (A-821).
- Reinsurance-related requirements are included, covering credit for reinsurance (A-785) and life and health reinsurance agreements (A-791).
- Other specialized product and valuation standards referenced include long-term care insurance (A-641), synthetic guaranteed investment contracts (A-695), preneed life insurance (A-817), minimum life and annuity reserve standards (A-820), and valuation of life insurance policies with new select mortality factors (A-830).

Conclusions and Implications: This index enables actuaries and regulators to quickly identify and locate the specific AP&P Manual Appendix A requirements applicable to a given product type or valuation issue when applying VM-A standards. It underscores the interconnected regulatory framework governing life insurance, annuity, and reinsurance reserve and nonforfeiture calculations, ensuring consistent application of NAIC model regulations across jurisdictions.

202601 VM-C.pdf.summary:
Title: VM-C: Appendix C - Actuarial Guidelines (Index)

Publisher and Published Date: NAIC (National Association of Insurance Commissioners), Valuation Manual (VM-C), publication date not specified in document

Purpose and Scope: This document serves as an index appendix to the Valuation Manual, cataloging Actuarial Guidelines carried over from Appendix C of the AP&P (Accounting Practices and Procedures) Manual. It provides a reference list of guideline numbers and titles addressing reserve calculation methods, interpretations of valuation laws, and specialized actuarial treatment for various life insurance and annuity products.

Key Points:
- Covers guidelines numbered I through XLVI (with gaps), addressing topics such as interpretation of the Standard Valuation Law, CRVM (Commissioners' Reserve Valuation Method), and CARVM (Commissioners' Annuity Reserve Valuation Method).
- Includes guidelines on specific product types: single premium deferred and immediate annuities, structured settlements, equity-indexed annuities and life insurance, variable life insurance, and guaranteed interest contracts (GICs).
- Addresses mortality table applications, including the 1980 CSO Mortality Table, select mortality factors, joint life functions, and preferred mortality tables.
- Contains guidance on specialized reserve issues: accelerated benefits, group long-term disability claim reserves, waiver of premium disabled life reserves, and reserves for companies in rehabilitation.
- Includes an appendix addressing New York State Insurance Department maximum reserve valuation and nonforfeiture interest rates.
- Document notes that a subsequent page is intentionally blank, indicating this is purely an index/reference page rather than substantive guideline content.

Conclusions and Implications: This index functions as a navigational and cross-reference tool directing actuaries and regulators to specific numbered guidelines within Appendix C for detailed technical requirements on reserve valuation methodologies. Users seeking substantive actuarial guidance must consult the individually referenced guidelines rather than this summary index for compliance and calculation details.

202601 VM-G.pdf.summary:
Title: VM-G: Appendix G - Corporate Governance Guidance for Principle-Based Reserves

Publisher and Published Date: NAIC Valuation Manual, not specified in document

Purpose and Scope: This document provides corporate governance guidance for insurance companies calculating principle-based reserves (PBR) under VM-20, VM-21, and VM-22. It defines the oversight roles of the board of directors, senior management, and qualified actuaries, while clarifying that certain companies passing exclusion tests or using the Alternative Methodology are exempt from some sections.

Key Points:
- Section 1 defines scope, key terms (group of insurance companies, board, senior management), and exemption conditions from Sections 2 and 3.
- Section 2 outlines board responsibilities: overseeing internal controls and infrastructure, reviewing reports/certifications, interacting with senior management, and documenting actions in meeting minutes.
- Section 3 details senior management duties: establishing infrastructure, reviewing valuation assumptions/methods/models, ensuring adequate internal controls, validating data and resources, and reporting to the board at least annually on governance matters, including certifications on internal controls and investments.
- Section 4 assigns qualified actuaries responsibility for overseeing PBR calculations, verifying assumptions/methods/models comply with the Valuation Manual, certifying prudent estimates with margins, providing summary reports to the board/senior management, preparing the PBR Actuarial Report (per VM-31), and disclosing unresolved issues to auditors/regulators.
- Qualified actuaries are not required to opine on aggregate reserve adequacy, surplus, or future financial condition unless serving as appointed actuary under VM-30.
- Governance documentation must be retained for at least seven years and made available upon request.
- Exempt companies still have limited reporting obligations regarding exclusion test risks and Alternative Methodology readiness.

Conclusions and Implications: This guidance operationalizes governance accountability for PBR by delineating distinct but interconnected responsibilities among boards, senior management, and qualified actuaries, without creating new legal duties beyond existing law. It ensures transparency, internal control validation, and documented oversight, reinforcing reliability and regulatory compliance in principle-based reserve calculations.

202601 VM-M.pdf.summary:
Title: VM-M: Appendix M - Mortality Tables

Publisher and Published Date: National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), Valuation Manual; dates as referenced within (table adoptions ranging from 1980 to 2018)

Purpose and Scope: This appendix defines and catalogs the mortality tables authorized for use in statutory valuation and nonforfeiture calculations, along with industry experience-based valuation basic tables. It provides formal definitions, source citations (NAIC Proceedings, SOA Transactions), and, where applicable, calculation methodologies for applying these tables.

Key Points:
- Defines "composite" (non-smoker-distinct) and "smoker/nonsmoker" mortality table categories.
- Section 1 lists valuation and nonforfeiture tables, including 1959 Accidental Death Benefits, 1961 CSI/CIET, 1980 CSO/CET (composite, smoker/nonsmoker, and blended versions), 1983 Group Annuity Mortality Table, 2001 CSO and 2017 CSO Mortality Tables (including Preferred Class Structure variants), Annuity 2000 Table, 2012 IAR Table, 2017 CSGI Table, 1994 GAR Table, and 1983 Table "a".
- Details the 2012 IAR Table methodology, combining the 2012 IAM Period Table with Projection Scale G2 via a specific formula, including correct rounding procedures (rounding must occur from the base 2012 rate for each projection year, not sequentially from prior rounded values).
- Section 2 covers Industry Experience Valuation Basic Tables: 2008 VBT, 2015 VBT (with Primary, Relative Risk tables for smokers/nonsmokers, select/ultimate and age-basis variants), 2012 IAM Basic Table, and GAM-94 Basic Table.
- Each table entry includes precise definitional language, developing organizations (SOA, Academy task forces), and citation to NAIC Proceedings or SOA Transactions pages.

Conclusions and Implications: This appendix serves as the authoritative reference for identifying and correctly applying specific mortality tables in actuarial valuation work under the Valuation Manual. Practitioners must use the exact table definitions and calculation methods (e.g., rounding rules for generational tables) specified here to ensure regulatory compliance and consistency in reserve calculations.

202601 VM-V.pdf.summary:
Title: VM-V: Statutory Maximum Valuation Interest Rates for Formulaic Reserves

Publisher and Published Date: NAIC (National Association of Insurance Commissioners), Valuation Manual provision (effective for contracts issued after Dec. 31, 2017)

Purpose and Scope: This document establishes the statutory maximum valuation interest rates for income annuity contracts, structured settlements, supplementary contracts, and related payout features used in CARVM/CRVM reserve calculations, superseding prior guidance in AG-9-B and AG-9-C. It applies to immediate and deferred income annuities, structured settlements, fixed payout annuities from settlement options/annuitizations, and related group annuity certificates issued after Dec. 31, 2017, excluding variable annuities and SET-covered contracts under VM-22.

Key Points:
- Defines "reference period," "jumbo contract" ($250M+ initial consideration), "initial age," and credit-related terms (Table X spreads, expected default cost, expected spread) needed to compute rates.
- Contracts are assigned to one of four Valuation Rate Buckets (A–D) based on reference period length and, for life-contingent contracts, initial age.
- Premium determination dates vary by contract type (e.g., date consideration is committed, date of issue, or date account value reaches zero).
- Statutory maximum valuation interest rate formulas combine a Treasury-based reference rate, credit spread, default cost deduction, and a fixed 0.25% spread deduction; jumbo contracts use daily rates, non-jumbo contracts use quarterly rates (rounded differently).
- Companies may elect (with regulator approval) to apply jumbo-contract rates to non-jumbo contracts under specified conditions, and must apply this consistently going forward.
- Detailed methodology specified for calculating reference rates, spreads, default costs, and corporate bond yields, including annually updated weight tables (Tables 1–4) based on representative annuity cash-flow modeling.
- Special rules apply for group annuity certificates, including handling of undetermined payout forms.

Conclusions and Implications: VM-V provides a standardized, formula-driven approach for insurers to determine maximum valuation interest rates for reserving purposes, replacing older actuarial guidelines. Compliance requires careful contract classification (jumbo vs. non-jumbo, bucket assignment) and ongoing use of NAIC-published rates, spreads, and default costs, ensuring consistency and comparability across the industry while allowing conservative company-specific adjustments.

asop007_219_LifeHealthCashFlow.pdf.summary:
Title: Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 7 - Life or Health Cash Flow Analysis

Publisher and Published Date: Actuarial Standards Board, December 2025

Purpose and Scope: This ASOP provides guidance to actuaries performing actuarial services related to the analysis of life or health cash flow risks, including reviewing cash flow analyses performed by another party. It applies to organizations that accept, self-insure, or retain financial loss risk, including insurers, HMOs, securitization vehicles, and self-insured employers, but excludes property/casualty actuarial services, which were removed from scope during this revision and addressed instead through an expanded ASOP No. 20.

Key Points:
- Defines key terms (asset, cash flow, cash flow analysis, cash flow risk, liability, organization, scenario), replacing "insurer" with "organization" to reflect broader applicability to noninsurance risk-bearing entities.
- Requires cash flow analysis when mandated by law and directs actuaries to consider it for reserve/capital adequacy, product development, nonguaranteed element testing, risk transfer testing, investment strategy evaluation, and actuarial appraisals.
- Provides guidance on determining scope (assets, liabilities, or both), including considerations like notional assets, receivables, off-balance-sheet items, and reinsurance or other risk transfer transactions.
- Details factors for projecting asset cash flows (economic sensitivity, asset quality, investment strategy) and liability cash flows (historical experience, policyholder options, management practices).
- Addresses scenario selection, sensitivity testing, assumption interdependency, interim values (e.g., negative surplus), and reliance on other parties' data, models, or assumptions.
- Expands documentation and disclosure requirements, including required communications in actuarial reports referencing ASOP Nos. 23, 41, and 56.
- Effective for work performed on or after June 1, 2026.

Conclusions and Implications: The revision modernizes ASOP No. 7 by broadening applicability to noninsurance risk-bearing organizations, removing property/casualty content (now covered by revised ASOP No. 20), and clarifying guidance on scope, asset/liability projection factors, scenario testing, and reliance on third parties. Actuaries performing life or health cash flow analyses must incorporate these enhanced disclosure and documentation standards, ensuring consistency with related ASOPs like Nos. 22, 23, 41, and 56.

asop024_217_LifeInsIllustrations.pdf.summary:
Title: NAIC Life Insurance Illustrations Model Regulation (Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 24, Revised Edition)

Publisher and Published Date: Actuarial Standards Board, adopted September 2024 (effective for actuarial services performed on or after December 1, 2024)

Purpose and Scope: This standard provides guidance to actuaries performing actuarial services in support of certifications or representations that life insurance illustrated scales conform to the NAIC Life Insurance Illustrations Model Regulation (Model) or applicable actuarial guidelines (AG 49, AG 49-A). It does not apply to determining a currently payable scale, which falls instead under ASOP Nos. 2 or 15.

Key Points:
- Introduces the term "applicable actuarial guideline (applicable AG)" and requires actuaries to consider such guidelines, including AG 49 and AG 49-A, when assessing conformity with the Model.
- Provides detailed guidance on setting experience factors underlying the disciplined current scale, covering investment return, hedge costs, mortality/morbidity/policyholder behavior, direct sales and other expenses, taxes, methodology changes, other lines of business, and consistency among factors.
- Adds new guidance on hypothetical index accounts, self-support and lapse-support testing, and treatment of policies in force one year or more.
- Expands guidance on reliance on data, projections, models, other parties' assumptions/methods, and other actuaries, cross-referencing ASOP Nos. 23, 41, and 56.
- Retains illustration actuary certification requirements (notice of inability to certify, notice of certification errors) and adds documentation and disclosure requirements tied to section 3 guidance.
- Deletes prior sections on appointment as illustration actuary and illustrated scale requirements, replacing certification disclosure guidance with a reference to applicable law.

Conclusions and Implications: The revision updates ASOP No. 24 to reflect AG 49-A and evolving indexed-product designs, clarifying actuarial responsibilities for experience factor selection, testing, reliance, and disclosure. Actuaries preparing or relying on life insurance illustrations must apply this updated guidance to ensure illustrations remain compliant, transparent, and well-documented.

asop027_211_PensionAssumptions.pdf.summary:
Title: Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 27 - Selection of Assumptions for Measuring Pension Obligations

Publisher and Published Date: Actuarial Standards Board, December 2023 (Doc. No. 211)

Purpose and Scope: This ASOP provides guidance to actuaries selecting, or advising on the selection of, assumptions used to measure defined benefit pension plan obligations, and also applies to assumptions used in measuring retiree group benefits obligations under ASOP No. 6. It excludes social insurance program obligations covered by ASOP No. 32, as well as individual benefit calculations, benefit statement estimates, and nondiscrimination testing.

Key Points:
- Consolidates the prior ASOP No. 27 (economic assumptions) and ASOP No. 35 (demographic assumptions) into a single unified standard; ASOP No. 35 will be repealed upon this standard's effective date.
- Establishes a three-step assumption selection process: identify types of assumptions needed, consider general factors (relevant data, materiality, format, rounding, subsequent events), and select a reasonable assumption.
- Defines a "reasonable" assumption as appropriate for the purpose, reflective of relevant data, based on estimated future experience or market data (or both), and expected to have no significant bias, absent adverse deviation provisions or alternative risk-assessment purposes.
- Provides detailed guidance for selecting inflation, investment return, discount rate, compensation increase, retirement, termination, mortality and mortality improvement, disability, optional form of benefit, expense, and other assumptions (e.g., Social Security, COLAs, payroll growth).
- Requires consistency among assumptions, review of previously selected assumptions at each measurement date, and assessment of assumptions not selected by the actuary.
- Adds new guidance on reliance on other actuaries, reliance on expertise of others, and documentation standards.
- Expands disclosure requirements, including rationale for assumptions, changes in assumptions, mortality table currency, and treatment of subsequent events.

Conclusions and Implications: Effective for actuarial reports issued on or after January 1, 2025 with measurement dates on or after that date, this standard streamlines and harmonizes pension assumption-setting guidance, requiring actuaries to exercise and document professional judgment more transparently, particularly regarding reasonableness, consistency, and rationale disclosures across all assumption types.

asop040_212_XFactors.pdf.summary:
Title: Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 40 — Compliance with the NAIC Valuation of Life Insurance Policies Model Regulation with Respect to X Factors

Publisher and Published Date: Actuarial Standards Board, March 2024 (Doc. No. 212)

Purpose and Scope: This ASOP provides guidance to actuaries performing actuarial services related to adjusting deficiency reserve mortality rates using X factors under applicable law based on the NAIC Valuation of Life Insurance Policies Model Regulation (Regulation XXX). It applies to all actuaries involved in such work, not only the appointed actuary, and is effective for statements of actuarial opinion for reserves with valuation dates on or after September 15, 2024.

Key Points:
- The appointed actuary must confirm X factors comply with applicable law and, if any X factor is below 100%, must annually issue a supported opinion; reliance on other actuaries does not eliminate the need for an overall independent opinion.
- Guidance is provided on creating X factor classes based on risk characteristics (e.g., distribution channel, target market, gender, risk classification, policy size, reinsurance use) while balancing credibility of experience data.
- Detailed guidance covers determining anticipated mortality: evaluating company experience, blending it with other sources (affiliated, industry, reinsurance) using credibility methods, and adjusting for antiselection, lapsation, and reinsurance effects.
- Actuaries must periodically reassess anticipated mortality using statistical analyses, adjusting X factor classes individually and in aggregate as needed.
- X factors should reflect anticipated mortality without future improvement, incorporate appropriate margins, and must be adjusted if Model requirements are not met.
- Extensive disclosure requirements are specified for actuarial reports, covering methodology, data sources, X factor class composition, statistical analyses, reliance on others, and changes from prior reports.

Conclusions and Implications: The revised standard broadens applicability beyond the appointed actuary, updates guidance to reflect newer CSO tables and the NAIC Valuation Manual (including VM-20/VM-30), and significantly expands documentation and disclosure requirements to improve transparency and consistency in X factor determination and mortality assumption setting.

asop058_218_ERM.pdf.summary:
Title: Actuarial Standard of Practice No. 58 - Enterprise Risk Management

Publisher and Published Date: Actuarial Standards Board, December 2024

Purpose and Scope: This ASOP provides guidance to actuaries performing actuarial services related to developing, maintaining, or reviewing all or part of an enterprise risk management (ERM) framework. It replaces and consolidates ASOP Nos. 46 and 47, applying to common ERM components such as governance, risk identification and classification, risk appetite, risk mitigation, risk metrics, capital management, stress testing/scenario analysis, and ORSA, but excludes actuarial services tied to specific ERM-related activities not intended to build or assess an ERM framework (e.g., product pricing, liability valuation).

Key Points:
- Defines key ERM terminology, including available capital, emerging risk, ERM framework, governance, internal capital assessment, ORSA, risk appetite framework/limit/statement, risk classification, risk inventory, risk taxonomy, and the "Three Lines" governance model.
- Requires actuaries to understand their governance role (including line-of-defense placement and independence) when performing ERM services.
- Provides guidance on risk identification, risk classification, and building/evaluating a risk appetite framework, including limits and triggers.
- Addresses evaluation of risk mitigation strategies, development/modification of risk metrics, and internal capital assessments.
- Covers stress testing and scenario analysis for resiliency testing, risk appetite limits, and capital/liquidity management processes, cross-referencing ASOP No. 55.
- Provides guidance on ORSA performance and ORSA report content/signatory responsibilities.
- Establishes rules for reliance on other parties (data, models, prescribed or non-prescribed assumptions) and documentation requirements.
- Section 4 specifies required and additional disclosures in actuarial reports, including confidentiality protections.

Conclusions and Implications: ASOP No. 58 modernizes and unifies prior ERM guidance (ASOP Nos. 46 and 47) into a single standard reflecting current ERM practice, terminology, and the interconnected nature of risk identification, appetite-setting, and mitigation. It is effective for actuarial services performed on or after May 1, 2025, after which ASOP Nos. 46 and 47 are repealed, requiring actuaries engaged in ERM-related work to align their practices and disclosures with this updated framework.

2024-IAIS-ICS-Level1-Level2.pdf.summary:
Title: Insurance Capital Standard - Level 1 and Level 2 Texts

Publisher and Published Date: International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS), December 2024

Purpose and Scope: This document sets out the Insurance Capital Standard (ICS), a group-wide prudential capital framework for Internationally Active Insurance Groups (IAIGs), combining high-level Level 1 principles with detailed Level 2 implementation specifications. It covers the perimeter of the ICS calculation, valuation of assets and liabilities, capital resources, capital requirements, and tax treatment to promote globally consistent supervision and comparable capital outcomes across jurisdictions.

Key Points:
- Establishes general principles of substance over form, proportionality, and look-through for assessing risk in collective investment vehicles and indirect exposures.
- Defines the perimeter of the ICS balance sheet, starting from audited consolidated GAAP financials, with rules for segregating insurance versus non-insurance entities and consolidation adjustments.
- Introduces the Market-Adjusted Valuation (MAV) approach, including current estimate cash flow projections, discounting via a Three-Bucket yield curve methodology (General, Middle, Top Buckets), and a Margin over Current Estimate (MOCE).
- Details capital resources classification into Tier 1 (Unlimited/Limited) and Tier 2 (Paid-Up/Non-Paid-Up) instruments based on loss absorbency, subordination, permanence, and availability criteria, plus deductions, adjustments, and composition limits.
- Specifies the standard method for calculating capital requirements across Insurance risk (life and non-life), Market risk, Credit risk, and Operational risk, using stress-based and factor-based approaches, aggregated via correlation matrices to a 99.5% Value-at-Risk target over one year.
- Provides guidance on risk mitigation recognition, geographical segmentation, management actions, tax effects, and alternative methods including internal models and SOCCA.

Conclusions and Implications: The ICS provides a comprehensive, granular framework enabling supervisors to consistently assess group-wide capital adequacy of IAIGs, enhancing comparability and cross-border supervisory cooperation. Implementation requires IAIGs to undertake detailed balance sheet adjustments, valuation recalculations, and risk charge computations, with significant judgment permitted through proportionality and management action provisions.

2025-IAIS-Application-Paper-AI-Supervisi.summary:
Title: Application Paper on the Supervision of Artificial Intelligence

Publisher and Published Date: International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS), 2 July 2025

Purpose and Scope: This paper supports insurance supervisors in applying existing Insurance Core Principles (ICPs) to the growing use of AI systems in insurance, without introducing new standards. It provides guidance, examples and good practices covering governance, risk management, robustness, transparency and fairness considerations for AI use across the insurance value chain, applicable to both insurers and intermediaries.

Key Points:
- AI adoption in insurance brings benefits (better risk assessment, financial inclusion, tailored products, efficiency) but also risks such as bias, opacity, uninsurability, cyber security threats, third-party concentration, and intellectual property concerns.
- Adopts the OECD's 2024 definition of an AI system, emphasizing autonomy and adaptiveness as distinguishing features from traditional models.
- Advocates a risk-based and proportionate supervisory approach, with criteria (outcomes-related and model-related) to classify AI systems by risk level and calibrate governance intensity accordingly.
- Reinforces governance and accountability expectations (ICPs 5, 7, 8, 16): Board/Senior Management oversight, corporate culture, human oversight, third-party/outsourcing management, and traceability/record-keeping.
- Addresses robustness, safety and security (testing methods like stress testing, adversarial testing, concept drift monitoring) and cyber security measures specific to AI, including GenAI/LLM risks (hallucinations, data leakage, model manipulation).
- Covers transparency and explainability (e.g., SHAP, LIME) tailored to different stakeholders (consumers, auditors, supervisors), and fairness/ethics considerations including data management, monitoring outcomes, redress mechanisms, and societal impacts of granular risk pricing.
- Includes an annex with real-world examples from IAIS members (EU AI Act, NAIC, EIOPA, MAS, NYS DFS, HKIA, UK) illustrating practical supervisory approaches.

Conclusions and Implications: Existing ICPs remain adequate for supervising AI in insurance, but supervisors and insurers must adapt existing governance, risk management, and conduct frameworks to address AI-specific risks proportionately. The IAIS will continue monitoring AI developments and update guidance as the technology and its adoption evolve.

2026-NY-SCL-spec_con_letter.pdf.summary:
Title: Special Considerations Relating to December 31, 2026 Reserves and Other Solvency Issues

Publisher and Published Date: New York State Department of Financial Services, August 3, 2026

Purpose and Scope: This letter applies to life insurers, fraternal benefit societies, and accredited reinsurers doing business in New York, providing filing instructions, additional testing and documentation standards, and guidance on actuarial opinions and asset adequacy analysis for reserves as of December 31, 2026.

Key Points:
- Establishes filing deadlines and procedures for actuarial opinions/memoranda, RAAIS, RBC C3 analyses, and extension protocols; requires prior approval for aggregating asset adequacy results across lines of business.
- Details required interest rate scenarios, including three modified scenarios (gradual down, down/up, pop-down) supplementing Regulation 126's standard scenarios, plus a 500 bps pop-up sensitivity test.
- Mandates specific assumption standards: lapse rate caps/formulas for term life, universal life with secondary guarantees, deferred annuities (dynamic lapse via calculated spread formula), and payout annuities (2012 IAR Table).
- Requires a 20% immediate equity drop with 5.5% annual recovery for volatile assets, net yield pick-up caps versus Treasury spreads, prepayment/default assumption justification, and disclosures on illiquid asset valuation (private equity, private credit).
- Specifies separate treatment for variable annuities with GMDBs/VAGLBs, equity-linked products, accelerated underwriting mortality (110% floor), and MVA annuities/Regulation 128 synthetic GICs.
- Requires interim (book value) surplus testing with mandatory additional reserves for shortfalls; lists 20 additional review criteria (Item 14) addressing tax offsets, reinsurance, hedging, inflation floors, and IMR treatment.
- Introduces "Special Sensitivity Tests" for risk assessment (not necessarily reserve-driving) covering lapse, mortality, and interest rate stress scenarios.

Conclusions and Implications: Insurers must incorporate these prescribed assumptions, sensitivity tests, and documentation requirements into their 2026 asset adequacy analyses; failure to meet "moderately adverse conditions" standards or address interim shortfalls may result in Department-required additional reserves following examination.

2023-12-NAIC-AI-Model-Bulletin.pdf.summary:
Title: NAIC Model Bulletin: Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems by Insurers

Publisher and Published Date: National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), template bulletin for adoption by individual state insurance departments (date not specified)

Purpose and Scope: This model bulletin reminds insurers licensed in a state that decisions or actions affecting consumers made or supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems must comply with existing insurance laws, including unfair trade practice and unfair discrimination statutes. It sets forth regulatory expectations for governance of AI development and use, and describes the information/documentation regulators may request during examinations or investigations.

Key Points:
- Cites legislative authority including the Unfair Trade Practices Model Act, Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Model Act, Corporate Governance Annual Disclosure Model Act, Property and Casualty Model Rating Law, and Market Conduct Surveillance Model Law.
- Defines key terms: AI, AI System, Algorithm, Adverse Consumer Outcome, Generative AI, Machine Learning, Model Drift, Predictive Model, and Third Party.
- Insurers are expected to develop, implement, and maintain a written AI System (AIS) Program covering governance, risk management, and internal audit functions, proportionate to the risk and potential consumer harm of each AI use case.
- AIS Program should address the full AI life cycle (design through retirement), across all insurance functions (underwriting, pricing, claims, marketing, fraud detection), including third-party AI systems and data, with due diligence, contractual audit rights, and monitoring.
- Governance expectations include board/senior management accountability, documentation standards, bias/data quality controls, model validation/testing, and consumer notice of AI use.
- Section 4 details specific documentation regulators may request during examinations, including AIS Program materials, model inventories, data governance records, validation/testing results, and third-party contracts/audits.

Conclusions and Implications: Insurers must ensure AI-driven decisions comply with existing insurance regulations regardless of the technology used, and should proactively establish documented governance and risk management frameworks. Failure to demonstrate adequate AI oversight may expose insurers to regulatory scrutiny, market conduct actions, or enforcement for unfair trade practices or discriminatory outcomes.

2021-IAA-IAN100-IFRS17.pdf.summary:
Title: International Actuarial Note 100 - Application of IFRS 17 Insurance Contracts

Publisher and Published Date: International Actuarial Association (Association Actuarielle Internationale), August 2021

Purpose and Scope: This educational document assists actuaries in understanding and applying IFRS 17 Insurance Contracts and ISAP 4 by offering practical examples and Q&A-style explanations. It is organized into 5 sections and 17 chapters covering classification, measurement, presentation, and disclosure requirements, based on the May 2017 Standard and June 2020 amendments, reflecting TRG discussions from 2018-2019.

Key Points:
- IFRS 17 applies to insurance contracts issued, reinsurance contracts held, and certain investment contracts with discretionary participation features, effective for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023.
- The General Measurement Approach (GMA), or "Building Block Approach," requires unbiased probability-weighted estimates of future cash flows, discounted for time value of money, adjusted for a risk adjustment for non-financial risk, and offset by a Contractual Service Margin (CSM) that eliminates day-one gains.
- Simplified approaches exist: the Premium Allocation Approach (PAA) for short-duration contracts, and the Variable Fee Approach (VFA) for contracts with direct participation features.
- Chapter 1 addresses classification, contract boundaries, and level of aggregation (portfolios, groups, combined contracts); Chapters 2-6 cover cash flow estimation, discount rates, risk adjustment, aggregation, and CSM/loss components.
- Additional chapters address reinsurance, fair value measurement, business combinations, transition methods (retrospective, modified retrospective, fair value), embedded derivatives, contract modifications, and presentation/disclosure requirements.
- The document emphasizes materiality and proportionality principles from ISAP 1, and notes that IFRS 17's principle-based nature allows for judgment and potential differences in interpretation across entities.

Conclusions and Implications: IAN 100 does not impose obligations but provides a reference framework helping actuaries navigate IFRS 17's complex, principles-based requirements, highlighting areas requiring significant judgment (e.g., contract boundaries, risk adjustment, discount rates) and referencing complementary IAA monographs for deeper technical guidance.

2026-02-NAIC-FABN-primer.pdf.summary:
Title: Funding Agreement-Backed Notes

Publisher and Published Date: NAIC Capital Markets Bureau; undated (references cite Fitch Ratings October 2025 and February 2026 publications, and S&P Global December 2025 publication)

Purpose and Scope: This report explains the structure, growth, and risks of funding agreement-backed notes (FABNs), securities issued by special purpose vehicles (SPVs) and backed by funding agreements from U.S. life insurers. It covers how FABNs work, why insurers use them, associated risks and mitigants, and evolving variations of the FABN structure.

Key Points:
- FABNs allow insurers to extend spread-based business and diversify funding sources by issuing funding agreements to a bankruptcy-remote SPV, which issues notes (mostly fixed-rate) to investors such as money market funds, pension funds, and asset managers.
- FABN ratings generally mirror the issuing insurer's financial strength rating; noteholders rank pari passu with other insurance policyholders in insolvency.
- FABN issuance has grown significantly, with record volume in 2025 driven by favorable market conditions, expanding issuer participation, and increased investor demand.
- Key risks include credit risk, operational leverage, liquidity risk, asset-liability mismatches, and transparency risk; mitigants include match-funding of terms, interest rate/currency swaps, and typically non-puttable, bullet-maturity structures.
- No statutory reporting requirement currently exists specifically for FABNs, limiting regulatory visibility into insurer exposure; the NAIC has proposed enhanced disclosure standards.
- Evolving structures include foreign currency FABNs (FXFABNs), funding agreement-backed commercial paper (FABCP), repurchase agreements (FABR), loans (FABL), and municipal prepay/energy bonds (FABMBs), each with distinct risk profiles.

Conclusions and Implications: FABNs are a growing, stable funding and income source for U.S. life insurers, but their expansion and structural diversification raise concerns about operational leverage, liquidity, and transparency. Enhanced regulatory disclosure is being pursued to improve visibility into insurer exposure and asset-liability matching within these programs.

2025-03-NAIC-MM-CLO-primer.pdf.summary:
Title: Middle Market Collateralized Loan Obligations Primer

Publisher and Published Date: NAIC Capital Markets Bureau, 2025

Purpose and Scope: This primer explains middle market collateralized loan obligations (MM CLOs), a subsector of the CLO market backed by loans to small and medium-sized companies. It covers collateral characteristics, structural features, risks and mitigants, investment advantages, and statutory accounting treatment for U.S. insurers.

Key Points:
- MM CLOs are typically balance sheet transactions in which asset managers securitize loans they directly originated, often retaining the equity/first-loss tranche to align interests with investors.
- Underlying collateral consists mainly of first-lien loans to smaller companies (often under $100 million EBITDA), which are privately rated or assigned credit estimates, lack secondary market liquidity/transparency, but tend to have stronger covenants than broadly syndicated loans (BSLs).
- MM CLOs carry larger credit enhancement than BSL CLOs (subordination typically 40%-46%, median ~42%), reflecting weaker collateral credit quality, and use O/C and I/C tests/triggers to protect investors.
- Structural flexibility includes PIK interest deferral options and financial maintenance covenants, providing lenders negotiating leverage and borrowers financial flexibility.
- MM CLO loans offer wider spreads (~200 bps more than BSLs) and higher yields, appealing to yield-sensitive investors, particularly life insurers, and driven by growth in private credit markets.
- Under SSAP No. 26/No. 43, MM CLOs are generally reported as asset-backed securities if they have substantive credit enhancement; otherwise, they are reported on Schedule BA as Other Invested Assets.
- Appendix data show MM CLOs are a smaller ($125 billion) but growing share of the CLO market versus BSL CLOs ($875 billion), with rising new issuance shares (up to 23.4% in 2023).

Conclusions and Implications: MM CLOs offer insurers attractive yield and diversification opportunities but require careful risk assessment due to limited transparency, lower-rated collateral, and specialized structures. Their growing prevalence in insurer portfolios underscores the importance of understanding statutory reporting requirements and credit enhancement mechanisms.

2024-NAIC-Private-Credit-primer.pdf.summary:
Title: Private Credit Primer

Publisher and Published Date: NAIC Capital Markets Bureau, 2024 (analysts Jennifer Johnson and Michele Wong)

Purpose and Scope: This primer explains the nature, growth, and structure of the private credit market and evaluates the associated risks and benefits for institutional investors, particularly insurance companies. It provides context on market size, key strategies, investor participation, and emerging risks as the market evolves.

Key Points:
- Private credit consists of non-publicly traded debt or debt-like securities extended mainly to middle-market firms by non-bank lenders, including insurers, private debt funds, and business development companies.
- It offers higher yields and spreads than public bonds/loans to compensate for illiquidity, limited secondary markets, and lack of transparency, while allowing customized loan terms and faster execution.
- Key strategies include direct lending (largest, ~40% of the market), distressed debt, venture debt, mezzanine finance, special situations, and a newly emerging category—fund financing.
- The market, estimated at $1.3–$1.7 trillion, is U.S.-dominated (~4.5% of the total U.S. credit market) and has grown roughly 16% annually since 2006, largely post-2008 financial crisis as banks retreated from middle-market lending.
- Growth projections vary: Moody's estimates ~$2 trillion by 2027; Preqin projects $2.7 trillion and BlackRock $3.5 trillion by 2028.
- Major investors include pension funds, insurers, and sovereign wealth funds; large asset managers (e.g., Blackstone, Ares, Oaktree, HPS, Goldman Sachs) hold significant "dry powder," raising concentration concerns flagged by the Federal Reserve.
- Risks include illiquidity, infrequent valuation, limited transparency, potential credit quality deterioration, and uncertainty about whether historical strong performance will persist as the market scales and evolves toward more complex, structured transactions.

Conclusions and Implications: As private credit expands in size and complexity—potentially incorporating more esoteric, lower-quality, and structured transactions—its historical strong performance may not be replicated in future, less benign credit environments. The NAIC Capital Markets Bureau will continue monitoring private credit trends given insurers' growing exposure and the market's evolving risk profile.

2025-SOA-LIMRA-VA-RILA-behavior-study.pd.summary:
Title: 2022-2024 Variable Annuity Behavior Study

Publisher and Published Date: Society of Actuaries (SOA) Research Institute Individual Annuity Experience Committee (IAEC) and LIMRA, March 2026

Purpose and Scope: This study jointly conducted by the SOA Research Institute and LIMRA examines Variable Annuity (VA) contract owner behavior for calendar years 2022-2024, updating a prior 2019-2021 study. Seventeen companies representing approximately 45% of industry new premium contributed data covering roughly 11.5 million surrender exposure contracts, $1.5 trillion in surrender exposure by contract value, over 620,000 surrenders, and $56 billion in withdrawals, including both single- and flexible-premium U.S. products with or without guaranteed living benefit riders.

Key Points:
- Average issue age of annuitants is trending higher over time; non-qualified contracts show average issue ages 4-5 years higher than qualified contracts.
- Nominal in-the-moneyness (Benefit Base/Contract Value >100%) declined by observation year across age groups but remained higher than in the 2019-2021 study.
- About half of GLWB-rider contracts took withdrawals, higher for qualified contracts; roughly three-fourths of these were systematic withdrawals. For non-GLWB contracts, about one-fourth took withdrawals, with only one-third systematic.
- Withdrawal rates rise sharply at ages 70+ for qualified contracts due to RMDs; non-qualified withdrawal rates are lower than qualified but higher than Roth IRA at older ages.
- Contracts without GLWB riders received markedly higher additional premium deposits in contract years 2-10, with the largest share of additional deposits occurring in year two.
- Surrender rates spike substantially in the year surrender charges expire, especially for out-of-the-money contracts, with year-over-year increases in 2023 and 2024; GLWB-activated and systematic-withdrawal contracts show notably lower surrender rates.
- Surrender rates rose across all benefit utilization levels from 2022-2024, lowest among the most efficient benefit utilizers.

Conclusions and Implications: The findings provide updated behavioral assumptions—regarding withdrawals, premium persistency, and surrenders—for actuaries pricing, valuing, and managing risk on VA products with living benefit guarantees. Detailed data and subsegment analysis are available via a 2025 Experience Studies Pro subscription.

2026-SOA-Individual-Payout-Annuity-Morta.summary:
Title: Individual Payout Annuity Mortality Experience Study (2020-2024)

Publisher and Published Date: Society of Actuaries Research Institute (Individual Annuity Experience Committee) and LIMRA, 2025 (study covers calendar years 2020-2024)

Purpose and Scope: This joint SOA Research Institute/LIMRA study presents mortality experience for individual payout annuities from 2020 through 2024, enabling comparison to standard valuation tables and population mortality. It updates the prior study covering 2014-2019, drawing on data from 26 companies (23 parent groups), representing over 80% of industry sales.

Key Points:
- The current study covers 3.1 million contract-years, $33.7 billion in annual income-years, and 143,190 deaths, versus 4.3 million contract-years, $33.6 billion in income-years, and 236,331 deaths in the prior six-year study.
- Average annual income per contract rose from $7,800 to $11,000.
- The overall A/E ratio versus the 2012 IAM Basic Table (amount basis) was 99.6%, down from 104.7% previously; versus the 2012 IAM Basic Table with improvement scale G2, it was 108.4%, similar to 108.7% previously.
- By sex, amount-based A/E ratios (2012 IAM Basic) were 100.1% (Female) and 99.1% (Male); with G2, 107.5% (Female) and 109.4% (Male).
- A/E ratios (2012 IAM Basic G2, amount basis) generally exceeded 100% across attained age groups except ages 65-74 (80% for 65-69, 92% for 70-74).
- A/E ratios generally decline as annual income increases, ranging from 126% (income below $2,500) to 91.5% (income $50,000+), with a minor exception for the $35,000-$49,999 band.
- Methodology excludes secondary annuitants while primary annuitants are alive, excludes substandard and structured settlement annuities, and uses age-nearest-birthday, amount-weighted experience.

Conclusions and Implications: Payout annuity mortality experience has shifted modestly relative to standard tables, with lower raw A/E versus 2012 IAM Basic but consistent results when mortality improvement (G2) is applied. These findings inform actuarial assumption-setting for pricing, reserving, and mortality improvement assumptions; detailed subsegment results are available via a paid data package.

2024-SOA-LIMRA-TermWL-Lapse-Surrender.pd.summary:
Title: 2015-2022 Term and Whole Life Insurance Policy Surrender/Lapse Experience Study Report

Publisher and Published Date: Society of Actuaries (SOA) Research Institute and LIMRA, December 2024

Purpose and Scope: This joint SOA Research Institute/LIMRA study analyzes policyowner lapse and surrender behavior for Whole Life and Term life insurance products over seven study years (2016-2022, covering policy anniversaries 2015-2022). It updates industry benchmark data on combined surrender and lapse activity, breaking out experience by attained age, issue age, policy year, product features, and, where possible, level versus post-level periods for term products.

Key Points:
- Twenty-eight companies contributed data, representing about 40% of industry term sales and 47% of industry whole life sales during the study period; only fully underwritten, single-life U.S. policies are included (workplace, simplified/guaranteed issue, and joint policies excluded).
- The study covers approximately 135.9 million policies exposed, 5.4 million surrenders/lapses, $30.6 trillion in face amount exposed, and $1.4 trillion in surrendered/lapsed face amount.
- Whole Life accounts for over 60% of exposure by count but only about 18% by face amount, due to smaller average policy sizes; 20-Year Level Term has the highest exposure among level premium term products.
- Whole Life lapse rates peak in the $25,000-49,999 face amount band, generally increase with face amount above that band (except flattening between $250K-$2.999M), and decrease with policy size in early policy years.
- Level term lapse patterns vary by product and duration: count-based rates often exceed amount-based rates early in the level period, with reversals occurring near and after the level period ends; lapse rates rise one to two years before level period expiration.
- Annual Renewable Term shows increasing lapse rates with issue age, with amount-based rates typically exceeding count-based rates.

Conclusions and Implications: The study provides updated, granular industry benchmarks for term and whole life lapse/surrender behavior, useful for pricing, reserving, and assumption-setting; more detailed results are available for purchase via the Experience Studies Pro Standard Data Package.

2025-10-Colorado-Reg-10-1-1-AI-Governanc.summary:
Title: Regulation 10-1-1 — Governance and Risk Management Framework Requirements for Life Insurers', Private Passenger Automobile Insurers', and Health Benefit Plan Insurers' Use of External Consumer Data and Information Sources, Algorithms, and Predictive Models (3 CCR 702-10)

Publisher and Published Date: Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies, Division of Insurance; new rule effective November 14, 2023, amended effective October 15, 2025.

Purpose and Scope: This regulation establishes governance and risk management requirements for insurers authorized in Colorado that use external consumer data and information sources (ECDIS), algorithms, and predictive models in insurance practices. It applies to insurers offering individually issued life insurance, private passenger automobile insurance, and health benefit plans.

Key Points:
- Defines ECDIS broadly to include credit scores, social media, location, purchasing habits, education, licensures, court records, IoT/telematics data, biometric data, and derived risk scores (excluding medical records for health insurers).
- Requires a risk-based governance and risk management framework overseen by the board or a board committee, with senior management accountability and a cross-functional governance group.
- Mandates documented policies covering ECDIS/algorithm/model design, testing, validation, complaint handling, risk prioritization, inventories with version control, change documentation, quantitative testing for unfair discrimination (particularly regarding race), ongoing performance monitoring, third-party vendor selection, and annual reviews.
- Insurers using third-party vendors remain responsible for compliance; vendors may submit documentation directly to the Division.
- Sets differentiated compliance and reporting deadlines: life insurers (framework available Dec. 1, 2024; progress report June 1, 2024); auto and health insurers (framework available July 1, 2026; progress report Dec. 1, 2025); annual compliance reports thereafter, signed by an officer, limited to 10 pages.
- Insurers not using ECDIS/algorithms must file an attestation; those beginning use later must submit required reports before deployment.
- Reports must be filed via SERFF as "Annual Report" filings; confidentiality protections apply per § 10-3-1104.9(3)(d), C.R.S.

Conclusions and Implications: Insurers must build and document robust governance structures to detect and remediate unfair discrimination arising from ECDIS-driven algorithms and predictive models, with escalating reporting obligations and officer attestations. Noncompliance may trigger civil penalties, cease-and-desist orders, or license suspension/revocation, underscoring the regulation's enforcement seriousness.

2024-2025-NAIC-Principles-Based-Bond-Def.summary:
Title: NAIC Principles-Based Bond Definition Package (2024-2025)

Publisher and Published Date: National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), Statutory Accounting Principles (E) Working Group — SSAP No. 26R adopted August 13, 2023; SSAP No. 21R revisions adopted March 16, 2024; both effective January 1, 2025

Purpose and Scope: This package establishes a principles-based framework for determining whether an investment security qualifies for reporting as a "bond" under statutory accounting, replacing the prior SSAP No. 26R. It covers SSAP No. 26R (Bonds), which addresses issuer credit obligations and related accounting/measurement guidance, and companion revisions to SSAP No. 21R (Other Admitted Assets) governing debt securities and residual tranches that fail to qualify as bonds.

Key Points:
- A bond must represent a creditor relationship with a fixed payment schedule, qualifying as either an "issuer credit obligation" (repayment from an operating entity's general creditworthiness) or an "asset-backed security" (repayment from defined collateral cash flows), per SSAP No. 43R.
- Debt instruments collateralized by equity interests carry a rebuttable presumption of not being creditor relationships unless equity risk is sufficiently redistributed/predictable.
- ABS status requires (1) meaningful cash flows from collateral beyond sale/refinancing and (2) substantive credit enhancement (subordination, overcollateralization, guarantees) placing holders in a different economic position than direct asset ownership.
- Structured notes and principal-protected securities are excluded from bond treatment; SVO-Identified Bond ETFs receive special treatment, including an optional "systematic value" measurement method.
- Detailed guidance covers amortized cost, yield-to-worst for callable bonds, impairment (OTTI), income recognition, prepayment penalties, and extensive disclosures.
- SSAP No. 21R addresses non-qualifying debt securities and residual tranches/first-loss positions, requiring Schedule BA reporting at lower of amortized cost or fair value, with admittance tied to underlying collateral quality.
- Detailed transition guidance applies for reclassifications occurring January 1, 2025.

Conclusions and Implications: Insurers must reassess all debt-like investments against this substance-over-form framework, potentially reclassifying holdings between Schedule D-1 (bonds), SSAP No. 43R (ABS), or Schedule BA (non-qualifying/residual assets), affecting capital, surplus, and RBC treatment starting in 2025.

2026-Synthesis-IFRS18-for-Insurers.pdf.summary:
Title: IFRS 18 for Insurers: Overview and Implications

Publisher and Published Date: ValAct_RAG knowledge base (original synthesis); no fixed publication date given — draws on secondary commentary dated between September 2025 and May 2026

Purpose and Scope: This document provides an original secondary-source overview of IFRS 18, "Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements," focusing on its implications for insurers who currently report under IFRS 17. It is explicitly not a reproduction of the primary IFRS standard text, which is restricted to eIFRS subscribers, and should be verified against the primary standard before use in any filing position.

Key Points:
- IFRS 18 was issued by the IASB in April 2024, replaces IAS 1, and is effective for annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027 (early adoption permitted), applied retrospectively with restated comparatives.
- It is a presentation/disclosure standard only — it does not change measurement of insurance contracts, which remains governed by IFRS 17.
- It mandates a five-category income statement structure (operating, investing, financing, income taxes, discontinued operations) and introduces two new subtotals: "operating profit" and "profit before financing and income taxes."
- Insurance finance income/expense must be classified within "operating," regardless of business model, with limited exceptions for equity-method investments — a specific concession sought by insurers during standard development.
- IFRS 18 creates a regulated "Management-Defined Performance Measures" (MPM) disclosure regime requiring description, methodology, reconciliation to the nearest IFRS subtotal, and tax effects for any non-IFRS metric (e.g., adjusted operating income, core/underlying earnings) published externally.
- Insurers must map IFRS 17's own prescribed line items (insurance revenue, insurance service expense, insurance finance income/expense) into IFRS 18's five categories and new subtotals; IFRS 17's measurement model itself is unaffected.

Conclusions and Implications: Insurers, having just completed IFRS 17 transition (effective 2023), now face a second major presentation-level change by 2027, requiring evaluation of current presentation practices, a transition/restatement plan, and preparation of investors and analysts for how familiar non-GAAP metrics will be reconciled and disclosed under the new MPM regime.

2026-03-BMA-Guidance-Note-Recovery-Plann.summary:
Title: Guidance Note for Recovery Planning Requirements

Publisher and Published Date: Bermuda Monetary Authority, 20 March 2026

Purpose and Scope: This Guidance Note explains the Authority's expectations regarding the structure and content of Recovery Plans required under the Insurance (Prudential Standards) (Recovery Plan) Rules 2024, which became operative 1 May 2025. It applies to insurers designated by the BMA based on nature, scale, complexity, financial stability risk and enhanced supervisory monitoring status.

Key Points:
- Recovery planning is an active, ongoing process (not a one-off compliance document) involving board and senior management engagement, and should be embedded within the insurer's Enterprise Risk Management framework rather than duplicating the CISSA.
- Proportionality applies to both development (e.g., phased submission) and maintenance (e.g., adjusted update frequency) of Recovery Plans, at the Authority's discretion.
- Bermuda insurers within a group may apply to adopt a Group Recovery Plan instead of preparing a standalone plan, subject to BMA approval and access to relevant group plan sections.
- Accountability for the Recovery Plan cannot be outsourced; the board and senior management retain ultimate responsibility even if development work is outsourced.
- Minimum required content includes: an executive summary, description of the insurer (structure, key services, dependencies), a tiered trigger framework (solvency, liquidity, quantitative/qualitative indicators), governance arrangements (development, approval, escalation, activation), a range of credible and feasible recovery options (capital raising, liquidity measures, cost reduction, divestment, run-off, etc.), scenario analysis and operational testing, and a communication plan covering internal and external stakeholders including the BMA.
- Recovery Plans must be reviewed/updated at least every three years or upon material change, and tested periodically for effectiveness.

Conclusions and Implications: Insurers must treat recovery planning as a substantive, integrated risk management exercise—supported by robust governance, testing and communication protocols—to enhance policyholder protection and financial stability, with the Authority retaining discretion over scope, proportionality and supervisory intervention.

2026-08-BMA-CP-IAIG-Supervision-Rules-20.summary:
Title: Consultation Paper: Proposed Insurance (Internationally Active Insurance Group Supervision) Rules 2026

Publisher and Published Date: Bermuda Monetary Authority (BMA), 21 August 2026

Purpose and Scope: This consultation paper sets out the BMA's proposed Insurance (Internationally Active Insurance Group Supervision) Rules 2026, intended to embed qualitative ComFrame standards into Bermuda's regulatory framework for Internationally Active Insurance Groups (IAIGs). It focuses on governance, enterprise risk management (ERM), and supervisory reporting/coordination, operating as an overlay to the existing group supervision framework rather than a standalone regime; ICS implementation and resolution framework development are being progressed separately.

Key Points:
- Places central accountability on the "Head of IAIG" for group-wide governance, risk management, strategy articulation (via the GSSA), board competence, and conflict-of-interest management.
- Introduces enhanced requirements for risk management and internal controls, including coordination of group-wide control functions (risk, compliance, actuarial, internal audit) and outsourcing due diligence.
- Requires a group-wide ERM framework for solvency purposes, including economic capital modeling, periodic independent review (at least every three years), an ERM evidence pack, and reinsurance/claims management strategies.
- Establishes expectations for identifying and monitoring intra-group transactions/exposures, contagion and concentration risks, and mandatory notification of significant intra-group risks.
- Sets group-wide investment governance expectations building on the Prudent Person Principle, including due diligence, intra-group investment criteria, and concentration monitoring.
- Introduces a comprehensive liquidity risk management framework covering stress testing, liquidity resource availability, contingency funding arrangements, and a liquidity evidence pack.
- Supports supervisory reporting, Crisis Management Group coordination, and cross-border supervisory cooperation.
- Poses three consultation questions on guidance needs, the overlay approach, and implementation challenges.

Conclusions and Implications: The BMA aims to align Bermuda's IAIG supervision with ComFrame while maintaining proportionality relative to existing group supervision rules. Following the consultation period (comments due 30 September 2026), the Authority targets publishing final Rules in Q4 2026, with continued parallel work on ICS and resolution frameworks.

2026-09-BMA-CP-Resolution-Regime-Commerc.summary:
Title: Consultation Paper – Proposed Phased Introduction of a Resolution Regime for the Bermuda Commercial Insurance Sector

Publisher and Published Date: Bermuda Monetary Authority, 15 September 2026 (comments due 15 December 2026)

Purpose and Scope: This consultation paper sets out the BMA's proposed phased approach to establishing a resolution framework for commercial insurers in Bermuda, aligned with FSB Key Attributes and IAIS ICP 12/ComFrame standards. It focuses on three foundational elements of the regime and invites stakeholder feedback ahead of future phases covering resolution powers, tools and cross-border cooperation.

Key Points:
- Proposes designating the BMA as the Resolution Authority (RA) for insurance sector entities, with governance safeguards to separate resolution decision-making from its supervisory role, enacted via amendment to the BMA Act 1969.
- Proposes five resolution objectives: protecting policyholders, protecting Bermuda's financial stability, minimising use of public funds, protecting client assets, and maintaining market confidence—applied flexibly without fixed priority ranking.
- Proposes scope covering domestic insurers and insurers designated as Internationally Active Insurance Groups (IAIGs) where BMA is group-wide supervisor, with discretion to include other Bermuda-domiciled insurers deemed critical to financial stability; scope to be enacted via amendment to the Insurance Act 1978.
- Not all in-scope insurers will require individual resolution plans; the RA, in consultation with Crisis Management Groups, will assess need based on nature, scale, complexity, substitutability, cross-border operations and interconnectedness.
- The framework will leverage existing BMA powers (e.g., Provisional Liquidation regime, recovery planning rules) and apply proportionality and risk-based principles to avoid undue regulatory burden.
- Raises four consultation questions on RA designation, resolution objectives, scope/planning criteria, and practical implementation issues.

Conclusions and Implications: This is the first phase of a multi-stage regulatory initiative; subsequent phases will address resolution powers, tools, planning details, cross-border cooperation and safeguards. Insurers and stakeholders should review and respond to the consultation, as outcomes will shape future legislative amendments and compliance obligations for Bermuda's commercial insurance sector.

2026-06-BMA-Stakeholder-Letter-Prudent-P.summary:
Title: Consultation Paper Response - Proposed Instructions and Guidance on the Application of the Prudent Person Principle

Publisher and Published Date: Bermuda Monetary Authority, undated (following December 2024 Consultation Paper)

Purpose and Scope: This document is the BMA's response to stakeholder feedback on its December 2024 Consultation Paper proposing enhancements to the Insurance Code of Conduct and Insurance (Group Supervision) Rules 2011 regarding the Prudent Person Principle (PPP). It applies to Bermuda's regulated commercial insurers (Classes 3A, 3B, 4, C, D and E) and insurance groups for which the BMA is Group Supervisor.

Key Points:
- The proposals aim to clarify BMA expectations for applying the PPP given growing use of illiquid, complex, structured, and related-party assets, and to reinforce board, senior management and control function responsibilities.
- Stakeholders requested clearer emphasis on proportionality; the BMA confirmed the Proportionality Principle is reaffirmed in the updated Guidance Note and compliance will be assessed case-by-case.
- The BMA rejected calls for a bifurcated regime for the property and casualty sector, noting the PPP already applies across sectors without distinction, though proportionality will guide assessment.
- For group structures, legal entity boards must retain demonstrable control and oversight even when relying on centralised group policies or functions.
- Investment risk should be assessed at portfolio level, but a "look-through" approach to underlying assets remains required, consistent with Insurance (Prudential Standards).
- GAAP valuations alone are insufficient to demonstrate PPP compliance; insurers must address all PPP elements, though GAAP procedures may support valuation review processes.
- The Code becomes effective upon issuance, with compliance required by insurers by 31 December 2026, allowing transition time.

Conclusions and Implications: The BMA has finalized its approach, incorporating proportionality considerations while maintaining core expectations largely unchanged. Insurers must prepare to demonstrate full PPP compliance—including look-through analysis and valuation governance beyond GAAP—by the December 2026 deadline.

2026-06-BMA-CP-Amendments-Code-of-Conduc.summary:
Title: Consultation Paper – Proposed Amendments to Insurance Code of Conduct, Insurance (Group Supervision) Rules 2011 and Insurance (Prudential Standards) (Insurance Group Solvency Requirement) Rules 2011 (with accompanying draft Insurance Code of Conduct and Guidance on the Application of the Prudent Person Principle)

Publisher and Published Date: Bermuda Monetary Authority, 09 June 2026 (comments due 27 July 2026)

Purpose and Scope: This consultation package sets out proposed amendments to the Insurance Code of Conduct (Code), the Insurance (Group Supervision) Rules 2011 (Group Rules), and the Insurance Group Solvency Requirement Rules, covering three areas: application of the Prudent Person Principle (PPP), enhancements to group supervision, and expansion of the Conduct of Business (COB) framework. It invites industry feedback ahead of finalization.

Key Points:
- PPP: Consequential amendments to Code sections (Investment/Liquidity/Concentration Risk, Credit Risk, Self-Assessment, Outsourcing) and to Group Rules (rules 5, 12, 13, 15), effective upon issuance with compliance required by 31 December 2026; accompanied by detailed Guidance on PPP covering investment strategy, risk management, governance, outsourcing, asset-liability matching, and complex/related-party assets.
- Group Supervision: Amendments to Group Rules (rules 2, 18, 21, new rule 33) and Group Solvency Rules, following the December 2024 CP and the Insurance Amendment (No.2) Act 2025 (effective 7 January 2026); new rules take effect 180 days after publication of final rules.
- COB Expansion: Scope broadened beyond domestic retail business to all Bermuda-registered insurers writing direct retail business to individuals anywhere, aligning international policyholder protections with domestic standards; amends Section 8 of the Code (fair treatment, intermediaries provisions); proportionality principle applies; 180-day compliance window post-final issuance.
- The full draft revised Code (June 2026) is included, detailing governance, risk management, outsourcing, and conduct of business requirements.

Conclusions and Implications: Insurers and insurance groups must review governance, investment risk management, and conduct-of-business practices to prepare for compliance deadlines (31 December 2026 for PPP-related changes; 180 days post-issuance for group supervision and COB amendments). Stakeholders are encouraged to submit feedback by 27 July 2026 before the BMA finalizes and issues the amended Code and Rules.

2025-09-BMA-Stakeholder-Letter-Public-Di.summary:
Title: Consultation Paper Response - Proposed Enhancements to the Public Disclosure Regime: Public Disclosure of Assets and Liabilities for Long-term Commercial Insurers

Publisher and Published Date: Bermuda Monetary Authority, 29 September 2025

Purpose and Scope: This letter summarizes stakeholder feedback received on the BMA's December 2024 Consultation Paper proposing enhanced public disclosure of assets and liabilities for Bermuda-regulated commercial long-term insurers (Classes C, D and E, excluding domestic insurers), and sets out the Authority's responses and next steps. The proposals aim to improve accessibility and detail of asset-related disclosures and strengthen transparency of investment portfolios to support policyholder decision-making.

Key Points:
- Stakeholders generally supported increased transparency but raised concerns about competitiveness, disclosure granularity, operational burden, and duration metric definitions.
- On competitiveness, the BMA will consider case-by-case, exceptional requests for modified (not waived) disclosures where registrants demonstrate an uneven playing field versus peer jurisdictions; an uneven playing field alone is insufficient justification.
- On granularity (e.g., CUSIP-level detail), the BMA maintains that detailed disclosure is necessary but will require qualitative questions on investment strategy and an auto-generated summary sheet to aid interpretation by non-expert users.
- On materiality/operational burden, the template will leverage existing returns (Lapse and Liquidity SBA Return, Bermuda Solvency and Capital Return) and GAAP-based financials; BMA will engage directly with run-off entities concerned about erosion of policyholder value.
- On duration metrics, the BMA accepted feedback to replace weighted average life with effective duration for both asset and liability disclosures, with further guidance to follow.

Conclusions and Implications: The BMA will publish draft Rules governing public disclosure requirements and an accompanying guidance document to support correct completion of the disclosure template. Insurers should prepare for enhanced, more granular asset/liability disclosure requirements, including effective duration calculations, while limited relief may be available only in exceptional, well-justified competitive circumstances.

2026-06-SOA-Obesity-Future-Mortality-Ess.summary:
Title: Obesity and Its Growing Impact on Future Mortality: A Collection of Essays

Publisher and Published Date: Society of Actuaries Research Institute, June 2026
